context_blurb:
The faster a windmill's sails spin, the harder the wind is blowing: the two are correlated, rising and falling together. Yet the sails do not make the wind. A correlation is a clue, not proof, and measurements can mislead too.

One trap is a confounder, a hidden third thing that drives both. A seaside town sells the most ice cream on its hottest days, when the most swimmers drown. Hot weather drives both, filling the ice-cream shops and the sea, so a ban on ice cream would hardly change the drownings.

In 1999 Graham Quinn and Richard Stone linked sleeping with a light on before age two to later nearsightedness, in which faraway things look blurred. In 2000 Karla Zadnik's team checked some 1,220 children and found nearsightedness about as common after a dark room as after a lit one. Nearsightedness runs in families, and nearsighted parents more often used night lights, so the parents' own eyes, a confounder, tied the lights to the children's.

Yet a link can be strong evidence. From 1951 Austin Bradford Hill and Richard Doll followed some 40,000 British doctors who had told them how much they smoked. Lung-cancer deaths rose step by step with the dose, the amount smoked, and such a dose-response pattern, more of a suspect bringing more harm, is hard to explain any other way.

The great statistician Ronald Fisher doubted that smoking was to blame. In 1958 he suggested that lung cancer begins years before it shows, with a slight inflammation that might lead a person to seek comfort in cigarettes. Fisher's idea turns the arrow round, the illness causing the smoking, and a link explained that way is called reverse causation. Fisher, a lifelong pipe smoker, was also a paid tobacco-industry consultant, and the evidence proved him wrong: doctors who gave up smoking went on to have far less lung cancer than those who kept on.

Chance makes links too. Setting thousands of yearly counts from public records side by side, the law student Tyler Vigen found American pool drownings rising and falling with Nicolas Cage's films from 1999 to 2009. Nothing ties films to drownings: compare enough pairs and a few will match by luck alone, so out of thousands, some rise and fall together by chance.

Precision is how closely repeated readings agree; accuracy is how close they come to the true value. Darts bunched tightly far from the bullseye are precise but not accurate, like a scale that shows the same wrong weight every time. Averaging cannot remove an error that repeats; only calibrating, checking and correcting the instrument against a known mass, can.

The Hubble Space Telescope's mirror, among the smoothest ever made, gave blurred pictures in 1990. The tool that tested the mirror's shape had been built wrong, one lens 1.3 millimetres out of place, so the polishers carefully ground it into the wrong shape. Every reading from that tool erred the same way: precise, but not accurate.

Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky asked which of two hospitals, one with about 45 births a day and one with about 15, logs more days when over 60 percent of the babies are boys. The small hospital does, because each day the share of boys wanders from one half by chance, and the fewer the babies, the farther it can wander. Four tossed coins come up three-quarters heads or more nearly a third of the time; a hundred coins almost never do, so bigger samples swing less.

In the usual telling, returning bombers had many holes in the wings and body but few in the engines, and the statistician Abraham Wald said to armour the engines. Wald assumed hits were spread over the whole plane, so the few engine holes meant that planes hit in the engines had mostly been lost: an engine hit often brought a bomber down. Studying only the survivors hides the losses, a trap called survivorship bias. That telling, with its red-dotted plane first drawn around 2005, simplifies Wald's real work, mathematical memos of 1943.

Bacteria multiply by splitting in two, each about every 20 minutes, so 100 become 200, then 400. The more there are, the more new ones each step adds, so on a graph marked in equal steps the points curve upward ever more steeply: exponential growth. Equal additions would make a straight line instead. When food runs low and wastes build up, growth slows and levels off.
